sp.p: I come along down to the guides, I will not follow you any more; they say you one mad, and so you is. I bleed of my nose; I choke of my breath; I sick of my stomach.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.p: Oh! all that's nothing.

sp.speaker: Louis.
sp.p: And the horrible dangers!

sp.speaker: John.
sp.p: Dangers! why didn't you tell me? I could go up the mountain with a cigar in my mouth and my hands in my breeches pockets.

sp.speaker: Louis.
sp.p: So you can still, if you like; those was all one little lies—one little lies—one little lies!

sp.speaker: John.
sp.p: Then, you great big liar, you shall come up, I swear.

sp.speaker: Louis.
sp.p: I swear! tu Dieu! corbleu! morbleu! ventre-bleu! sacrrrebleu! I cut the cord!

sp.speaker: John.
sp.p: Cut away, and go to the devil.

div.stage: (Both of them cut the cord and roll off on each side.)

div.head: Scene VI.
div.stage: Public room, Hôtel d'Angleterre: Mrs. Silverton; Sir Harry, holding worsted; Miss Scattergold, winding it.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Miss Scattergold, is that your trunk in the passage upstairs?

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Oh! the little one by the door? yes, that's mine.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Little one, by George! I could put one of my men in it.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Oh! but I've one in which you could put one of your men on horseback in it.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Haven't you one in which you could put all the king's horses and all the king's men?

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Nonsense! how awkward you are! Do hold your hands still, and don't jerk them so at the corners.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: It is you who pull on the curb so at the turns; you should give a fellow his head at the corners.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
Sir Harry.
sp.p: Yes, and mine, for I've forgotten half you told me you should want.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Yes; and I didn't tell you half either.

div.stage: (She gives him a long list.)

sp.speaker: Sir Harry
sp.p: Seven gowns from Worth.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: I only want seven a day to begin with, you know—one for breakfast, one for walking, one for driving, one for tea, one for dinner, one for the evening, and a ball-dress that I can't wear on any other occasion, you know.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry
sp.p: Five bonnets.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: No, that's a mistake, six; it should be six; that's enough, because you know there are the five hats—go on.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry
sp.p: Nine dozen pockethandkerchiefs.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: All right! three dozen plain, three dozen worked, and three dozen with lace.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry
sp.p: Three dozen boots, two dozen shoes, one dozen slippers.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: All right—go on!

sp.speaker: Sir Harry
sp.p: Twelve dozen pairs of gloves, four dozen—

div.stage: (She runs at him and snatches the paper from him.)

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Oh dear! was that all?

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: No, there's twice as much more.

div.stage: Enter Simperkin and Heavysides.

sp.speaker: Simperkin.
sp.p: Oh dear me! here is the howiedest, dweadfullest thing happened!

sp.speaker: Heavysides.
sp.p: Yes, two men fallen down the mountain.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: All the way down?

sp.speaker: Simperkin.
sp.p: Every inch of it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: Good Heavens! I hope it wasn't that good fellow, John Homespun?

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Oh! go—go—quick all of you, and find out, and come directly and tell us all about it!

div.stage: [Exeunt the men.
(Mrs. Silverton and Miss Scattergold winding wool.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: And so you've made up your mind at last?

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Well, it seems to me almost, at first, three months is a short time to make a lifelong engagement.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: Ah! but three months in the Alps are as good as three times three anywhere else for that sort of business; and you are really going to take that nice fellow, Harry, for better, for worse?

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: He shan't be worse, and he can't be better; but now, Fanny dear, tell me, you don't wish he'd married one of your own women instead of a Yankee girl, do you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: No, my dear friend, indeed I do not. Every knot and every tie, every hook and every eye, that brings our two countries nearer, and fastens them closer to each other, is good for the whole world. Heaven prosper their friendship, and avert their enmity for ever!

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Amen! There's a good deal of that same knotting and tying, and hooking and eyeing, going on just now between the opposite sides of the Atlantic.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: It's like marrying one's cousins, I fancy.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Grandchildren, you mean. Great grandchildren.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: Very great grandchildren!

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: And, you know, the forbidden degrees of relationship only go as far back as one's grandmother, and so I'm going to marry my great grandfather, and here he comes.

div.stage: Enter Sir Harry and the other men.

sp.speaker: Both the Women.
sp.p: Well, well! who? what? how? where?

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Some truth at the bottom, a mountain of flummery over it. It was that good fellow, Jack Homespun.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: Went up all the way to the top?

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Yes, plucky fellow that he is.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: And fell down all the way to the bottom?

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Oh no! not quite. Two parties of guides went up after him and the fellow who was with him, and brought them down safe.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: And sound?

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Well, sound enough for all present purposes, a little the worse for the tumble only: one eye nearly punched out, one arm almost broken, and one leg all but twisted off; but he is coming to the table d'hôte this evening, and swears he'll go home to-morrow.

div.stage: Enter all the Tourists, John and Louis with their eyes, arms, and legs bandaged. All the Tourists surround John and congratulate him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: I'm so glad to have shaken hands with you once more; you know, we start for home to-morrow.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.p: So do I.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: Shall you be able to travel?

sp.speaker: John.
sp.p: I shall travel whether I'm able or not.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: Then we shall all start together. That will be jolly!

sp.speaker: Louis' Ladies.
sp.p: We for Clapham.

sp.speaker: The Squeeze Family.
sp.p: We for Warwickshire.

sp.speaker: Miss Scattergold.
sp.p: I for the Langham Hotel.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Silverton.
sp.p: I for Hereford Square.

sp.speaker: Sir Harry.
sp.p: I for Knightsbridge Barracks.

sp.speaker: John.
sp.p: And I for Betsy.

div.stage: (Yodling chorus.)
